## What the 4 pinned conflicts actually are

"3–4 stale conflicts" has been quoted often enough that it deserves a breakdown. On the first live graph at rev 2,604, with the adoption pin applied, all four conflicts are staleness, and they are not all the same kind:

| node type | status | untouched | has note | has owner | |---|---|---|---|---| | `group` | in_progress | 7 d | yes | no | | `decision` | in_progress | 7 d | yes | no | | `issue` | in_progress | 5 d | yes | yes | | `task` | blocked | 3 d | yes | yes |

Two conclusions, the second less comfortable:

1. **Three of the four are real debt**: work items untouched for 3–7 days, owned, with notes. Nothing is wrong with the tool; the team has not closed them. Fixing them by editing status would make `audit` green without the work being done, which is why they stay visible. 2. **One of the four was a false positive**, and 0.7.7 fixed it: `group` nodes are long-lived by nature — a group marked `in_progress` stays that way for the life of the group, and its `updatedAt` does not move when its children change. The rule assumes a short-lived work item, so `group`, `env` and `member` (registrations, not work) are now exempt ([DECISIONS #20](decisions/20-staleness-applies-to-work.md)). The refusal to change it quietly is the point: audit output is a contract, so the change came with a decision, four tests and this note.

Measured after the fix, on the same graph at rev 2,610 (1,288 nodes): `audit --pin` reports **3 conflicts**, `pin match: true` — the three work items above, and no registry node. The unpinned count is 1,064, i.e. the legacy-evidence class grew with the graph.

Each of those conflicts is also a structured finding (`kind: stale_work_item`) carrying the node, its type, its status, its owner and `age_days` — so an agent can act on "whose item is 7 days old" without parsing the sentence (v0.9.0).

The threshold is configurable (`AMG_STALE_DAYS`, or `--stale-days` for one run), because "too long" depends on the team's cadence. On that graph it reads:

| threshold | conflicts | |---|---| | 3 days (default) | 3 | | 7 days | 1 | | 14 days | 0 | | 30 days | 0 |

A team that meets weekly would see three false alarms at the default; one that meets monthly would see none at 30. The tool cannot know which team it is, so it does not pretend to: default stays 3 (the original rule), the knob is one environment variable, and invalid values fall back to the default rather than silently disabling the check.

The unpinned `audit` on the same graph reports about 1,060 conflicts, which is also worth reading precisely: they are almost all "`done` without structured evidence", the legacy-format artefact — not 1,060 broken facts.

# Scheduling expiry (no daemon, on purpose)

`amg expire` is an explicit, idempotent command. This project deliberately ships **no long-lived scheduler process**, for three reasons:

1. A daemon inside the library would need its own failure model (restarts, overlapping runs, partial writes) — the file store already has an atomic write and an advisory lock, and cron inherits both for free. 2. Expiry is a decision with consequences. Keeping it as a command means it can be dry-run, logged, and replayed by hand. 3. An unknown validity window can never be auto-expired. A background process invites "just expire everything" defaults; a command does not.

## Safety properties you can rely on

- `amg expire` without `--apply` writes nothing (dry-run is the default). - `--apply` only touches nodes where the validity window is **known**, the `valid_until` has passed, and the node is not already superseded. - The action is `status: superseded` + `superseded_at` + one `op=expire` change record. Nodes are never deleted. - Running it twice is safe: the second run reports `applied 0`. - Nodes whose validity time is unknown (everything produced by `amg adopt`) are skipped and counted.

```cron # every day at 03:17: dry-run first, then apply, append to a log 17 3 * * * cd /srv/memory && amg expire ./mem > /var/log/amg-expire.log 2>&1 && amg expire ./mem --apply >> /var/log/amg-expire.log 2>&1 ```

```ini # /etc/systemd/system/amg-expire.service [Service] Type=oneshot WorkingDirectory=/srv/memory ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/amg expire ./mem --apply ```

```ini # /etc/systemd/system/amg-expire.timer [Timer] OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:17:00 Persistent=true

Expiry does not delete anything, so rollback is a normal write: re-open the node with `amg status <id> done --note "expiry reversed: <reason>"` (a status change requires a note by design), and correct the validity window if it was wrong. The original node and its `op=expire` change record remain in the graph either way, so the reversal is itself auditable.

## What would have to change to justify a daemon

- Multiple writers per graph, where a cron run could overlap a human write. The advisory lock serialises them, but a daemon could batch and back off. - Graphs large enough that a full load per run is expensive. - A need for sub-minute expiry precision.

None of these holds at the sizes measured in `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` (10k nodes, read paths under 100 ms).

Scope: `agent-memory-graph` v0.3.0 — the CLI, the Python library, and `amg mcp` (the stdio MCP server). Written before implementing read-only mode, so the guarantee below is stated with its limits instead of implied.

This document describes **what the software can and cannot protect**. If a threat is not listed as mitigated, assume it is not mitigated.

## 1. What is being protected

| Asset | Where it lives | What it leaks | |---|---|---| | Node content (labels, notes) | `graph.json` → `nodes[]` | Project state, decisions, issue text | | Evidence pointers (`locator`, `content_sha256`) | `graph.json` → `nodes[].evidence[]` | File paths, URLs, command lines, content hashes | | Transaction history | `graph.json` → `changes[]` | Who wrote what, when, and with which note | | Read log (opt-in) | `reads.jsonl` | Query text and the fact that a high-risk read happened | | Audit pin | wherever the caller put it | Hashes of id lists; not secret, but integrity-relevant |

`graph.json` is **plain, human-readable JSON**. There is no encryption at rest and no key material anywhere in this project.

``` OS user ──(the only real boundary)── │ nothing inside this box authenticates anyone │ CLI ──┐ │ lib ──┼──> Memory ──> Store ──> graph.json mcp ──┘ │ ```

There is exactly **one** enforcement boundary that matters: the operating system's file permissions for the user running the process. Everything above it is convenience. Concretely: any process running as the same user has the same authority over the memory as the memory's owner. The CLI, the library and the MCP server are three doors into the same room, and none of them has a lock.

`amg mcp` opens **no socket and no port** and makes no outbound request. It speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout. If you put a network transport in front of it, you have removed the only boundary the system has, and this document no longer applies.

- **A1 — the user.** Fully trusted. Nothing here defends against them. - **A2 — a local client of the same OS user.** A coding agent, a script, an editor plugin. Untrusted *in intent* but fully trusted *in capability*: it can also just open the file. - **A3 — a prompt-injected A2.** An agent that was told by page content, an issue body or a tool result to write to memory. This is the actor read-only mode exists for. - **A4 — another OS user / a network peer.** Outside the boundary. Only file permissions and the absence of a listener stand in the way. - **A5 — the supply chain.** Zero runtime dependencies, so the surface is the Python standard library. `amg mcp` does not import third-party code.

| # | Threat | Status | Where | |---|---|---|---| | T1 | A2/A3 writes a node through `amg mcp` to plant a false "done" conclusion | **Mitigated by `--read-only`** (two layers) | §5 | | T2 | A2/A3 bypasses the evidence gate or IR-2/IR-4 by going through MCP instead of the CLI | **Mitigated by construction**: no tool has its own write path; all call `Memory`, and `Memory` raises | §6 | | T3 | A2/A3 overrides history: rewrites `changes[]`, or edits a `done` node back to `open` without a note | **Partially mitigated**: the API refuses, a file writer does not | §7 | | T4 | A2/A3 exfiltrates the whole memory with `memory_search`/`memory_digest`/`memory_audit` | **Not mitigated.** Reads are readable | §7 | | T5 | A2/A3 reads `reads.jsonl` to learn what the user looked at | **Not mitigated** (same directory, same permissions) | §7 | | T6 | Denial of service: hold the write lock forever | **Partially mitigated**: `LockTimeout` after the configured wait (exit 3), and the lock is released when the handle closes, so a crashed process cannot wedge the graph | `store.py` | | T7 | Crash during write leaves a half-written graph | **Mitigated**: full write to a temp file + `fsync` + `os.replace`, so a reader sees old or new, never a mix | `store.py::_atomic_write` | | T8 | Dangling/duplicate writes corrupt structure | **Mitigated**: `check` (IR-1..IR-4) and the write gates reject them before commit | `protocol.py`, `gate.py` |

### Evidence authenticity is declared, not proven (v0.20.0)

`content_sha256` is supplied by the caller; the write gate checks its shape (64 lowercase hex) and nothing else. A fabricated hash is accepted, yields `anchor_state: "present"`, and that is the first retrieval sort key — reproduced in the public package (`issue.mem-arch-evidence-sha-forgeable`, severity high). Two-part response, both shipped: **disclosure** here and in `docs/API.md` (`present` = *declared*), and an **observation mechanism**, `amg verify-evidence`, which re-hashes `path:` locators and exits 1 on mismatch. Deliberately not fixed: no per-read verification (I/O on the hot path, and referenced files legitimately move); no `anchor_state` split into `verified`/`claimed` (without a persisted verification result that would be a label, not a measurement); `cmd:`/`url:`/`sha256:` evidence cannot be checked offline and is reported `unverifiable`, never a pass. Path confinement (v0.21.0): `path:` evidence must resolve inside the graph directory; absolute and `..`/symlink paths are `outside_root` and never hashed, so a public store cannot be used as a hash oracle for files it does not own (`issue.mem-arch-evidence-locator-out-of-tree`). Treat `--strict` as "anchored as declared".

## 5. Read-only mode: what it guarantees

`amg mcp <dir> --read-only` (and `Memory.open(dir, read_only=True)`) provides:

1. **Tool refusal before dispatch.** `memory_add`, `memory_status` and `memory_supersede` raise `E_READ_ONLY` and are reported to the client as `isError: true`. The call never reaches the `Memory` method. 2. **Commit refusal as a backstop.** A read-only `Memory` raises `E_READ_ONLY` in `_commit()`, the single function every mutation funnels through. This is the layer that matters: a future mutating method cannot forget the check, and a tool added later without being classified is still blocked here. 3. **No write tools advertised.** `tools/list` returns the five read tools only, and `initialize` carries a `read-only` instruction string so an agent client is told the constraint instead of discovering it by failing. 4. **No bytes written.** Tested by hashing `graph.json` before and after a session that attempts every write tool, and after calling `add_node`, `set_status`, `supersede` and `expire(apply=True)` directly.

- It is not authentication. It does not identify the client, and it cannot stop a client from launching a second `amg mcp` **without** the flag. It reduces the blast radius of one session; it does not deprive the OS user of authority. - It is not a sandbox. `A2` can still `open("graph.json","w")`. - It does not block disclosure: all read tools keep working, by design. - It does not cover the legacy `amg adopt`/`amg migrate` entry points, which are writes by nature and take no read-only flag.

Honest summary: **`--read-only` protects the graph from the process it was started in, and from the agent driving that process. Nothing more.**

## 6. Why MCP cannot bypass the write discipline

The MCP layer adds no validation and no write path of its own. Every tool calls the same `Memory` method the CLI calls, so:

- evidence format and the conclusion gate (`E_EVIDENCE_MISSING`, `E_EVIDENCE_FORMAT`) fire identically over MCP; - `IR-2` (real source) and `IR-4` (conclusion-`done` needs evidence) are enforced in `Memory._make_node`, below the transport; - a rejected write returns `isError: true` with the protocol code in the text, never a success frame.

`tests/test_mcp.py` asserts the error comes back as a tool error; `tests/test_readonly.py` asserts the same for read-only refusals.

## 7. Accepted risks (not bugs to report)

- **Same-user file access.** Anyone who can run a process as the user can read and rewrite the graph. The only defence is OS permissions, disk encryption, or keeping the file out of shared locations. - **No tamper evidence inside the file.** `changes[]` is append-only *by the API*, not cryptographically. A process with file access can rewrite it. `amg fingerprint` / `amg verify` (§7a) detect accidental corruption and edits that leave state and history inconsistent, but the digest can be recomputed by the same attacker. Real evidence requires an external witness: commit the fingerprint into git, a CI log, or another host, and compare out of band.

### 7a. What `amg verify` does and does not buy

`amg fingerprint` emits `state_sha256` (nodes+edges, order-independent) and `history_sha256` (`changes[]`, in order). `amg verify --expect FILE` exits 1 when either differs from the recorded value.

| Situation | Detected? | |---|---| | Bit rot, partial write, truncated file | yes (state digest) | | A node edited in the file with no change record | yes — state moves, history does not | | A change appended without touching nodes | yes — history moves, state does not | | An attacker who rewrites state **and** history and recomputes the digest | **no** — only an external witness catches this | | An attacker who also rewrites your copy of the fingerprint | **no** |

This is why the project does not ship an in-file hash chain over `changes[]`: it looks stronger than it is (the attacker regenerates the chain in one pass) while costing a schema migration, and it invites people to trust it.

### 7b. Checking that the boundary still holds

Because permissions *are* the boundary, `amg doctor` checks the conditions under which the boundary stops existing: `SEC_WORLD_WRITABLE`, `SEC_GROUP_WRITABLE` (info), `SEC_NETWORK_PATH` (SMB/NFS/UNC — the advisory lock is not reliable there), `SEC_GRAPH_SYMLINK`. `amg doctor --strict` exits 1 on a warning (`E_INSECURE_GRAPH`); `amg mcp` prints the warnings to stderr at startup and keeps serving.

It is a check, not a sandbox: it cannot make a shared filesystem safe, only refuse to be quiet about it. - **Read tools are unlimited.** `memory_digest` accepts `max_bytes`; the others have no output bound beyond `k`. A client can read everything available. - **`reads.jsonl` is a plain-text log** of query text for high-risk reads. Do not treat it as a secret store (see SECURITY.md). - **Timing/resource limits.** A very large graph makes `audit`/`digest` slow; the tool has no per-request timeout.

## 8. Authorization: decided out of scope, and what to do instead

Earlier versions of this file listed "authentication and multi-tenancy" as pending work. That was a deferred decision, not a plan. It is now decided: **this project will not implement authentication or per-caller authorization.**

The reasoning is not "it is hard". It is that, in this architecture, app-level authentication is bypassable in one step:

1. The memory is one file the caller can open. A process that can run `amg` can also `open("graph.json", "w")`. A token check inside `amg` therefore proves only that the caller *has the file* — which they already needed. 2. Single-user file stores typically end up with the token in a config file readable by that same user, so the check becomes decoration that costs code, tests and maintenance while changing no capability. 3. Anything that *would* hold — separate users, containers, read-only mounts, filesystem ACLs — is enforced below us by the OS. Re-implementing it above the file would be a weaker copy.

So the boundary is explicit and the work moves to where it actually holds:

| Need | What to do | |---|---| | Two people, one graph, different rights | two OS users + a group; make the file group-readable and directory group-writable only if you accept shared write | | An agent that must never write | `amg mcp --read-only` (blast radius for this session) **and** start that process as a user with no write permission on the file | | Several projects, no leakage between them | one graph directory per project; separate mounts if the projects have different trust levels | | Read-only dashboards / audits | serve a copy, or mount the directory read-only for that user | | Untrusted plugins or code | container or VM; not a flag |

What *is* implemented in this area: `--read-only` (one session), `amg doctor --strict` (refuses to stay quiet when the permission boundary does not hold: see §7b), and `amg fingerprint` / `verify` (tamper *detection*, §7a).

### What would change this decision

Three things, each of which invalidates the reasoning above rather than merely making auth more attractive:

- a network transport (then identity is unavoidable — and should be built by whoever ships the transport, not bolted on here); - multi-writer concurrency beyond the advisory lock (then "who wrote this" stops being answerable from the process); - a hosted or multi-tenant deployment (then tenant separation must be structural, i.e. separate stores, not a column in a shared file).

# Where the write cost goes (measured on the real graph)

The real-graph run ([`REAL-WORLD.md`](REAL-WORLD.md)) showed one write at **147 ms** on a 15.3 MB graph. This page answers the next question — *what would make it faster, and is any of it worth doing now* — by measuring the bytes and the time rather than guessing.

Source: the same live graph, adopted to `amg/v1` (1,249 nodes, 640 edges, 2,559 change records, 15,580,438 bytes). Numbers from `perf_counter`, three iterations.

| section | bytes | share | |---|---|---| | `changes[]` (event log) | 12,317,037 | **79.1%** | | `nodes[]` | 3,079,209 | 19.8% | | `edges[]` | 84,203 | 0.5% | | document overhead | 99,988 | 0.6% |

The history is four fifths of the file. Any plan that starts by trimming *nodes* is aimed at the small part.

## Where the time goes (one write = read, render, persist)

| step | time | |---|---| | parse `graph.json` (`json.load`, 15.6 MB) | 75.1 ms | | render (`json.dumps`, indent=2) | 50.3 ms | | `fsync` + replace | 22.5 ms | | **total** | **147.9 ms** |

Which matches the single `add_node` measured end to end (147 ms). The cost is dominated by moving 15.6 MB of JSON through the process **twice**, not by the disk.

## Options, with their measured payoff and their price

| option | measured payoff | price | verdict | |---|---|---|---| | **A. Cold-archive old nodes** (>30 d untouched) | **0 nodes qualify**: the oldest node in this graph is 6 days old, p50 = 1 day | a second file to keep consistent, plus audit coverage | **deferred** — nothing to reclaim today | | **B. Move old `changes[]` to a sidecar file** | nodes+edges only = 3.22 MB, render 6.7 ms (vs 50.3); estimated write ≈ 30 ms, i.e. **−80%** | breaks the single-file atomic property: two files, one `os.replace` no longer covers both; `check`/`audit`/`digest`/`fingerprint` must span files; copying a graph stops being one file | **not now** — see below | | **C. Compact JSON** (drop `indent=2`) | 15,209,100 bytes: **2.4% saved**, render 42.6 ms (vs 50.3) | destroys line-diffability, which is a stated design goal (graphs live in git) | **rejected** — 2.4% is not worth it | | **D. Incremental writes** (touch only changed regions of the file) | theoretical | abandons the crash guarantee ("a reader sees old or new, never a mix"); every write path would need a journal of its own | **rejected** — the atomicity guarantee is the product |

Nothing changes today. The trigger for revisiting stays the roadmap's:

> write p95 > 250 ms, **or** file > 20 MB, **or** nodes > 10k

Measured headroom: 147 ms / 15.6 MB against those thresholds — roughly two-thirds of the way on both axes, and growing at about 12 MB of history per 1,000 writes at this graph's density. When it trips, option **B** is the one with a real payoff, and its price is explicit: the graph stops being one copyable file, so `check`, `audit`, `digest` and `fingerprint` all gain a second input and the atomicity claim has to be restated rather than quietly weakened.

(Policy note: the earlier signed ruling forbids adding an escape hatch that becomes the default path — so there is no `--no-history` flag. If history ever moves, it moves for everyone, with the guarantees rewritten.)

```bash PYTHONPATH=src python3 - <<'PY' import json, os, sys, tempfile, time sys.path.insert(0, "src") from amg import Memory from amg.store import dumps src = "/path/to/legacy-graph.json" dst = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "mem") Memory.adopt(src, dst, group="probe") doc, path = Memory.open(dst).doc, os.path.join(dst, "graph.json") def ms(fn, n=3): t = time.perf_counter() for _ in range(n): fn() return round((time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1000, 1) print("parse", ms(lambda: json.load(open(path, encoding="utf-8")))) print("dumps", ms(lambda: dumps(doc))) print("sizes", {k: len(json.dumps(doc[k], indent=2).encode()) for k in ("nodes", "edges", "changes")}) PY ```

- One graph, one week of history, one machine (macOS). A graph with years of history would show a higher share for `changes[]`, not a lower one. - `fsync` cost depends on the filesystem; the 22.5 ms here is APFS on this laptop. - Option B's 30 ms estimate is a projection from measured parts (parse of 3.2 MB, render 6.7 ms, `fsync` of 3.2 MB), not an implemented and measured feature. It is labelled as an estimate for that reason.

**A synthetic noise model must be calibrated on what competes, not on what exists.** #50 left one question open: whether N2 — whose distractors are six tokens drawn from the queries' own vocabulary — represents the noise a long-lived memory graph meets. An attempt to answer it failed its own pre-registered calibration check, and the failure is the decision.

Measured on the candidates that actually compete (top-100, gold excluded), the contrast is real:

| corpus | pairs | mean coverage | median | share ≥ ¼ of the query | |---|---|---|---|---| | control (27 real nodes) | 146 | 0.147 | 0.167 | **0.144** | | n2 (query-vocabulary noise) | 2,578 | 0.415 | 0.400 | **0.918** |

The pre-registered plan was to build `N2-cal` whose competing distractors reproduce control's 0.144, by drawing each node's query-token count from control's per-pair coverage distribution. It produced 0.606, missed the ±0.10 tolerance, and by the rule fixed beforehand the corpus was rejected — so its `recall@5` of 0.654 is a rejected-run diagnostic, not a result. Probing an explicit token-count mix showed why the base rate cannot repair it: 0.55/0.43/0.02 gave 0.537, 0.70/0.28/0.02 gave 0.516, and 0.80/0.19/0.01 gave 0.497. **With two thousand nodes carrying two query tokens, those nodes own the top-100 however rare they are** — the pool is selected by the very quantity being calibrated, so a per-pair rate mapped into a 10k pool overstates competition by construction.

Decisions: **(a)** synthetic noise corpora in this project must be calibrated and checked on the *competing* subset, with the check run before any recall number is reported (the Q2 rule, now standing); **(b)** this attempt is recorded as a failure with its numbers and its probe ladder, not tuned until it agreed; **(c)** the next design samples distractor text from **real note text** (the team's graph holds 410 notes) instead of token soup, because the failure is in the generator's shape, not its parameters; **(d)** nothing about the published results moves — N2 stays the hardest corpus, `0.538` stays the shipped number, and the 0.70 target stays **unmet**.

Cost: one pre-registration, two 3-second corpus builds and a probe ladder, to replace "N2 might be unrepresentative" with a measured ratio (6.4×) and a concrete reason why the obvious re-calibration does not work. *Signed 2026-10-31; `experiments/retrieval_noise_representativeness/`; v0.33.2.*

**The +0.077 arm was a vocabulary filter, not content-word weighting — and #48's named direction was inferred from it.** Independent verification of v0.33.0–v0.33.2 reproduced every published number and then found one description that does not match its implementation.

#48 says: "Restricting coverage to content words only returns N2 to 0.615 (+0.077, the first arm to pass C2's +0.05) … the next direction is **content-word weighting or stop-word stripping**". The script behind that arm (`/tmp/re8/attack_coverage_mechanism.py`, reproduced here) does:

orig_vocab = frozenset(tokens of the original 27-node corpus) qt_eff = qt & orig_vocab # counted query tokens cov = len(qt_eff & node_tokens) / len(qt) # denominator stays the full query length

That is a **vocabulary filter** — it counts only query tokens that exist in the original corpus's own vocabulary — not a part-of-speech filter. Re-running the arms reproduces the numbers exactly: A −0.057, B −0.057, C **+0.077**, and the mechanism #48 records (distribution mismatch, `q04` pushed from rank 1 to 79) stands. What does not stand is the inference.

1. **The +0.077 was never an estimate for content-word weighting.** The filter knows which vocabulary is "original", so it encodes information a shipper would not have; it is partly oracle, and it is closer to the sentence #47 proposed ("separate source tokens from injected ones") than to the direction #48 named. Anyone reading #48 as "content-word weighting is worth about +0.08" would be reading a number that does not measure that. 2. **The direction was tested properly afterwards and failed.** #49's pre-registered round implemented real content-word coverage — stopword stripping with the denominator over content tokens — and every arm lost recall (0.442 / 0.404 / 0.481 against 0.538). So the error was in the *label*, not in the conclusion that closed the family: the family is closed for a stronger reason than the one #48 offered.

The page is not rewritten: the published sentence stays, with a dated correction appended that points here (a corrected claim is marked, never deleted). A test asserts that both the original sentence and the correction are present, so a later cleanup cannot quietly drop either.

Decisions: **(a)** experiment arms are described by their implementation, not by the idea they resemble — an arm name may not name a mechanism its code does not implement; **(b)** a correction to a published page requires a dated block on that page plus an entry here, and the original text stays; **(c)** #49's conclusion is unchanged and un-weakened: the lexical family is closed for N2.

Cost: one independent verification caught a mislabelled arm two releases after publishing; the cost of not catching it would have been a future round implementing "content-word weighting" and quoting +0.08 as its prior. *Signed 2026-10-31; `docs/memory-arch/VERIFY-V033X.md`; v0.33.4.*

**Discussed:** <member> — <evidence path>; <member> — <evidence path>

naming at least **two distinct members** and at least **one evidence path**. One of them proposed a variant or an attack; the other independently verified it; the CEO decides and signs, and writes the page. A page that cannot name them is not a decision but one agent reasoning in public.

`tests/test_group_authority_gate.py` enforces it mechanically, and the rule function is itself tested against four synthetic page bodies (missing line, one name, two names without a path, and a valid line), so the gate cannot pass by being vacuous.
